chunks.text: Wastewater is typically collected through sewage pipes in municipal areas. Treatment of wastewater entails a step-wise process that occurs in primary, secondary, and tertiary stages. Primary treatment involves basic screening and filtration processes to remove suspended solid waste and reduce its biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), which is an indicator to monitor water quality that assesses the amount of oxygen microorganisms must consume to break down the organic material present in wastewater (US EPA, 2012) . Primary treatment can reduce BOD by up to 30% (Flo ¨rke, 2013) . Secondary treatment uses biological processes to break down the dissolved organic matter remaining after primary treatment. Secondary treatment can remove up to 90% of BOD and total suspended solids (US EPA, 2004) . Any additional step in wastewater treatment is considered tertiary treatment (or ''advanced treatment''), which includes any purification process that continues beyond the previous steps and may require more complex technology such as ion exchange and reverse osmosis to further remove contaminants or phosphorous and nitrogen (World Bank, 2013b; US EPA, 2004) .

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: A pilot plant comprised of primary (DAF) and secondary treatment unit (two stage trickling filters) was set up by Li et al. (1984) . Each trickling filter was 2.4 m high and consisted of media (surface area-98 m 2 /m 3 ). Around 40-50% oil and grease removal were achieved from DAF system. In case of trickling filters organic matter removal efficiencies were 70-85%. Apart from that, nitrification also resulted, but the process was entirely dependent upon loading rates. Intensive studies by Banks and Wang (2004) have shown that loading rates plays a vital role in biological treatment. Intensive studies conducted by them have shown that the organic matter removal efficiencies were 60-85% when operated at OLRs of 1.2-8.1 kg BOD/ m 3 -d for nine trickling filters.

chunks.text: Belkacem et al. [29] reported the use of reverse osmosis for the treatment of groundwater with 95 % removal of TDS and 97 % reduction in conductivity. Srinivasan et al. [30] used spiral bound reverse osmosis membranes for recovery of phenolic compounds. The combination of NF and RO membrane have also been demonstrated which resulted in significant improvement in the removal of COD and TDS with decrease in conductivity. Nataraj et al. [31] used membrane-based nanofiltration and reverse osmosis process combination for treatment of distillery wastewater which resulted in 99.8 % TDS reduction, 99.9 % COD reduction and 99.99 % potassium removal. The use of the membrane process is associated with serval drawbacks like fouling, flux decline, secondary waste generation and requirement of repetitive chemical cleaning especially for the streams having higher COD concentrations [32] . The membrane bioreactor (MBR) is one of the important process for treatment of sewage water. However, membrane fouling has been reported as one of the major drawback of MBR due to activated sludge liquor, biological flocs and soluble colloidal compounds.

chunks.text: In order to recover the lipid-rich biomass from the treated wastewaters and to further reduce the level of COD in the respective wastewaters, microfiltration using a low-cost ceramic membrane (pore size: 1.01 μm and porosity: 44%) was carried out. Fig. 6 presents the membrane flux and COD removal (%) from the different wastewaters at various operating pressures in the range of 34-172 kPa. With an increase in the operating pressure, the flux of the microfiltration system increased due to a high driving force acting on the membrane surface. The membrane flux was lower for DWW and PPWW as compared with that for the BGWW due to membrane fouling. In general, the membrane fouling is attributed to concentration polarization on the membrane surface and blocking of pores in the porous ceramic structure. In case of DWW and PPWW, fouling of the membrane was observed due to the adsorption of organic solutes/lignin and membrane surface polarization that creates further resistance to the transport of liquid through the membrane [1] . On the other hand, the less viscous BGWW possesses persistent organics [22] , and hence do not affect the membrane flux largely.

chunks.citation: Jasper, JT et al. (2017). Toxic Byproduct Formation during Electrochemical Treatment of Latrine Wastewater. ENVIRON SCI TECHNOL.
chunks.text: Electrochemical treatment systems have been shown to provide effective treatment of latrine wastewater. Greater than 5-log inactivation of bacterial and viral indicator organisms is achieved via production of reactive chlorine species from chloride (15−20 mM) within 1 h at 4 V applied cell potential. 3 A combination of reactive chlorine species and direct oxidation provide reduction of chemical oxygen demand (COD) 4 and transformation of trace organic contaminants within 4 h (3.5− 4.5 V applied cell potential) 5−7 with rates enhanced at elevated chloride concentrations (up to 75 mM). Under similar operating conditions, ammonium removal occurs via breakpoint chlorination, 8 and phosphorus can be precipitated as hydroxyapatite. 9 Unfortunately, strongly oxidizing conditions in the presence of the high concentrations of chloride and organic matter typical of latrine wastewater also result in formation of toxic byproducts. 10 While wastewater disinfection is essential to protecting human health, an ideal electrochemical system should also be designed to minimize toxic byproduct formation. 11 Chloride enhances electrochemical treatment via formation of reactive chlorine species (e.g., hypochlorous acid, chloramines, and chlorine radicals).

chunks.text: The 378,000 m 3 /day (100 MGD) Advanced Water Purification Facility (AWPF) treats secondary effluent from the Orange County Sanitation District at capacity. Approximately 70% of the product water recharges groundwater using spreading ponds (basins) in Anaheim, California, which is blended with stormwater and imported/purchased water (OCWD, 2019a) . When the systems' capacity was 265,000 m 3 /day, water was produced at a unit cost of $0.56/m 3 (capital and O&M) and conveyance costs amounted to an additional $0.10/m 3 (Raucher & Tchobanoglous, 2014) .

chunks.text: The results showed a significant reduction in CFP for all three plants when influent wastewater underwent primary clarification before biological treatment. Specifically, plants A, B, and C experienced a reduction in CFP of 7.55%, 9.5%, and 10.59%, respectively. This is because greater particulate settling in the primary clarifier results in lower CO 2 emissions from microbial respiration and higher waste sludge  contents in the AD process (Gori et al., 2011 (Gori et al., , 2013)) . In terms of CO 2 emissions, the AD ranked third after PG, with 0.019, 0.039, and 0.34 kg CO 2 /kg COD rem. for plants A, B, and C, respectively. However, the incoming COD concentration to the AD of each system was significantly different. Plant C received almost 5.6 times lower COD than plant A, resulting in higher COD removal (78.75%) and concurrently larger CO 2 emissions.

chunks.text: A mass of 300 kg of screenings was sampled from the municipal wastewater treatment plant of Bourg-en-Bresse (Region Rhône-   Alpes, France). The waste was made of a mix of screenings from 15-mm and 3-mm screens and was compacted in the plant. The sample was taken to the laboratory where it was homogenized and divided into 20 sub-samples of 8 kg. The procedure allowed to guarantee a good reproducibility of the sub-samples composition, which was verified analytically. The samples were stored at À18 °C. A digestate sampled from a municipal solid waste (MSW) digester was used as an inoculum, in order to have active microflora and to make easier the start-up of anaerobic process. chunks.text: An equalization tank was designed to maintain airflow and homogenize the incoming  wastewater, with a maximum volume of 30,000 m 3 and a depth of 4 m. In the biological step, the MBR bioreactor, as a prominent innovation in wastewater treatment, was designed with a total membrane surface area of 4200 m 2 and a porosity of cake layer equal to 0.15 m 2 . This design facilitates the degradation of both organic and inorganic substances, reduces sludge production, and produces high-quality effluent. Moreover, the tank volume was set at 9740 m 2 , and the backwash frequency and flow rate were assumed to be 30 s and 2000 m 3 /d, respectively. Then, the RO technology was implemented to enhance and complete the wastewater treatment process. The RO membranes, characterized by their small pore size, effectively reject molecules and ions, resulting in purified water. The RO system contained four vessels with a membrane area per element of 35 m 2 /element. The assumed recovery rate for the RO system was 60 %, meaning that 60 % of the feed water was treated and converted into purified water.
